newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM navigates scandal minefield in parliament.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM navigates scandal minefield in parliament.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's new government has emerged from its parliamentary debut apparently unscathed by a Health Ministry scandal that has brought his own campaign finances under scrutiny.
Even the whiff of an ongoing scandal has not dented the public's backing for Hashimoto's cabinet, with a media poll on Wednesday showing a substantial rise in its support ratings.

Hashimoto has spent the last three days fielding opposition questions in both houses of parliament after he began the legislative session last week saying he felt "nothing but shame" at the widening Health Ministry scandal.

Police arrested former Vice Health Minister Nobuharu Okamitsu on Wednesday on charges that he took 60 million yen ($530,000) in bribe money from a business executive running specialised nursing homes for the aged.
The scandal highlighted close ties and alleged exchanges of cash for favours between bureaucrats and the industries they supervise.
Despite a start marred by the scandal, Hashimoto's government enjoys relatively high support ratings.
Support for Hashimoto's cabinet has risen to 56.5 percent from 45.6 percent three months ago, the Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper said on Wednesday.
The cabinet was launched last month with all its members from Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) even though the LDP failed to win a majority in October 20 general elections.
A Yomiuri survey conducted at the weekend showed the disapproval rating for the cabinet stood at 30.8 percent, down from 38.5 percent in September.

Hashimoto's former cabinet, before the general elections, included members of the Social Democratic and Sakigake parties, which decided not to join the new cabinet but agreed to enter a loose policy alliance with the conservative LDP.

Hashimoto and Health and Welfare Minister Junichiro Koizumi were targeted by the opposition for tough questioning over the health scandal because they received political donations from lobbyists with links to nursing home operator Hiroshi Koyama, arrested last month for allegedly bribing a health official.
Koyama was re-arrested on Wednesday over his ties to Okamitsu, formerly the ministry's top bureaucrat.

Koizumi has said he received 3.5 million yen ($30,900) from the lobby, while Hashimoto has acknowledged receiving a total of seven million yen ($61,900) in donations from the lobby and another group linked to Koyama.
Neither Hashimoto nor Koizumi has been accused of wrongdoing and both have said they properly reported the donations, which were legal.
Hashimoto kept a low profile in parliament over the issue, promising to exercise "greater discipline", but Koizumi was combative under opposition fire.
"Frankly, I take umbrage at talk claiming that donations which were properly processed are suspect," Koizumi shot back at a Japanese Communist Party legislator.

Even if the funding questions are not a problem, however, analysts say Hashimoto will face trouble passing the most important legislation of the parliamentary session, three bills to establish a nursing care insurance system for the elderly.

Takeo Nishioka, secretary-general of the opposition New Frontier Party, told parliament: "It was thoughtless of the government to submit the bills amid the current situation at the Health Ministry." ($1=113 yen)
